segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Isha in the original: two ca's, a saha, and tirtva, having crossed. Both kinds of knowing, carried across together. The next three verses will sound very familiar.

Songs do it constantly. The chorus comes back word for word, and then, the last time, one word changes, and that's the line that gets you. Why does the Isha seem to say the same three verses twice? Because it's doing the same thing. Andham tamah pravishanti ye asambhutim upasate. Into blind darkness enter those who worship not-becoming. Three verses back, the line said avidya. One word swapped, the frame held still, so the new word lights up.
screen: `THE LAST CHORUS CHANGES ONE WORD.` → `THE SAME THREE VERSES, TWICE?` → `ONE WORD SWAPPED.`

segments.voice: Lay them side by side. Where verse nine had avidya, not-knowing, verse twelve has asambhuti, not-becoming. Where nine had vidya, twelve has sambhuti: becoming, coming into being. Sam, together, and bhuti, being: things coming together into being. The darkness, the iva, the those-who: all unchanged. Verse thirteen echoes ten, right down to the same close: iti shushruma dhiranam, thus we have heard from the steady ones. Then verse fourteen echoes eleven: whoever knows both together crosses death by one and reaches the deathless by the other. But look closely. In fourteen, a new word steps in: vinasha, destruction, falling apart, right where the echo leads you to expect the other half of the pair. A frame that held for two verses bends at the third. Readers explain the swap in different ways, and a reader of the original doesn't need to settle it today. The skill is noticing. When a text almost repeats itself, the almost is where to look. That works on more than old verses. When a story you've heard many times comes back with one detail changed, that detail is where to lean in.
screen: `ONE WORD SWAPPED, THE FRAME STILL.` · `SAMBHUTI: COMING INTO BEING.` · `VINASHA STEPS IN.` · `THE ALMOST IS WHERE TO LOOK.`

segments.voice: Say one familiar line out loud, softly, three times: a line from a song, a verse, something someone always says. Each time, listen for what changes on its own, the pace, the breath, the weight on one word. Then sit with whichever version stayed with you.
Reading the Isha in the original, verses twelve to fourteen: sambhuti, becoming, an echo of the verses before, and vinasha, the word that breaks the pattern.
